# Small Decisions, Clear Structures

Author: Concept to Story contributors

Provenance: Original synthetic teaching text, created for this repository. Not a published book, scientific study, or quotation. All names, quantities, and study results below are invented for testing. Section labels are stable source locators; they are not PDF page numbers.

## Contents

1. Opportunity cost
2. Atomic updates
3. Conditional probability
4. Association and causation
5. Special obligations

## 1. Opportunity cost

When choosing among mutually exclusive feasible options, the opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone. It is not the sum of every rejected option. What counts as valuable depends on the decision maker and the relevant time horizon. A cost already incurred and not recoverable does not become a future benefit just because the decision maker wants to justify it.

To assess a choice, first identify what is feasible now and what cannot be done together. Then compare the best feasible alternatives using a stated criterion. Changing constraints or new information can change which alternative is best. The criterion may include rest or relationships rather than money alone.

## 2. Atomic updates

In this teaching model, a transaction changes a sender's stored balance and a recipient's stored balance together: either both changes commit or neither does. This is atomicity. A failure after only the debit must not leave a committed debit without its paired credit. The model assumes both balances participate in one transaction managed by a system that supports this property.

This claim alone does not establish isolation between concurrent transactions, durability after a committed write, or atomic behavior across unrelated external services. A human promise to do two tasks is not an implementation of an atomic transaction.

## 3. Conditional probability

For events A and B with P(B) > 0, P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Conditioning on B changes the reference group to cases where B holds. It does not in general make P(A|B) equal to P(B|A).

Consider 100 invented workshop participants. There are 40 beginners. Of the 30 people using blue notebooks, 18 are beginners. In this finite dataset, the fraction of beginners among blue-notebook users is 18/30, whereas the fraction of blue-notebook users among beginners is 18/40. The counts illustrate the definition; they do not establish causation or a population estimate without further assumptions.

## 4. Association and causation

An invented observational report followed 24 volunteers. People who chose to practice with flashcards had higher recall scores than those who did not. Participants were not randomly assigned. Prior knowledge and available study time were not controlled. The observation supports an association in this sample, not the conclusion that flashcards caused the difference.

The report does not prove that flashcards cannot help. It leaves the causal effect unresolved because other differences between the groups could explain the pattern. Both the positive causal claim and the claim of no possible effect would go beyond this report.

## 5. Special obligations

For this synthetic normative framework, an ongoing personal relationship can provide reasons for assistance that are stronger than reasons to help a stranger in an otherwise similar situation. These reasons do not automatically override every competing commitment, another person's consent, or all limits on cost. This is a proposed ethical framework, not an experimentally established fact or the only possible account of obligation.

Relationship-based reasons differ from keeping an exact ledger of exchanged favors. Assistance can be asymmetric when needs and abilities differ. Judging a particular refusal requires context, including the burden, other commitments, and the relationship; a single refusal does not determine a person's moral character.

## 6. Connection map

Sections 1 and 5 both involve competing claims on time or resources, but opportunity cost describes what is forgone while special obligations offers one normative account of which reasons matter. Section 2 concerns a technical all-or-nothing property rather than an ethical duty. Section 3 changes a probability reference group; section 4 concerns what conclusions a study design supports. These are parallel tools, not a single ladder of increasingly correct theories.
